dangerous_cpts.main_problem: This CPT sits at the key integration point between program-log inconsistency and the two local deviation aggregates. The failure patterns repeatedly pass through two specific columns of this CPT, and one of them has zero success support. Domain-wise, execution integrity should be strongly informed by program anomaly and response/dispatch deviations; however, the current table can still output Normal with high confidence when Program_Anomaly=No and both deviation nodes are No, and can output Compromised even when both deviation nodes are No if Program_Anomaly=Yes. Because this node directly drives Root_Causes, errors here can systematically propagate into repeated misdiagnosis. The evidence is stronger here than for upstream deviation nodes because the suspicious behavior is not fully explained by a single parent and reflects the fusion logic of this CPT itself.

suspicious_parameters.justification: Column 7 corresponds to Program_Anomaly=No, Deviation_in_Response=No, Deviation_in_Dispatch=No. This exact configuration recurs in failures, especially together with both deviation nodes selecting No. Although Normal is semantically reasonable in isolation, the zero success support and repeated downstream failures suggest the CPT may be too confident in treating the complete absence of detected anomalies as normal, likely underweighting hidden compromise cases.

Column 3 corresponds to Program_Anomaly=Yes with both local deviation aggregates at No. This pattern appears repeatedly in failures and indicates the CPT may over-translate isolated global log inconsistency into compromised execution despite no corroborating response/dispatch deviations. Since this is a fusion node, such overcommitment can independently distort final root-cause inference.

dangerous_cpts.main_problem: This CPT is the final diagnostic decision layer, so any miscalibration here directly creates wrong labels even if upstream reasoning is acceptable. Several activated root-cause parameters appear only in failures and not in successes. In particular, the table strongly favors FDI when Network_Manipulation=Yes, Execution_Integrity=Normal, Physical_Anomaly=No, and strongly favors System_Fault when Network_Manipulation=No, Execution_Integrity=Normal, Physical_Anomaly=Yes. These mappings are plausible in principle, but the repeated failure-only activations indicate the final class allocation may be too sharp or imbalanced relative to the domain, especially when evidence is mixed or partially missing.

suspicious_parameters.justification: Column 3 corresponds to Network_Manipulation=Yes, Execution_Integrity=Normal, Physical_Anomaly=No. The CPT assigns a strong preference to FDI. Repeated failure-only activation suggests the model may be overcommitting to FDI based mainly on network evidence while discounting alternative causes such as memory corruption or ambiguous conditions.

Column 6 corresponds to Network_Manipulation=No, Execution_Integrity=Normal, Physical_Anomaly=Yes. While System_Fault is domain-consistent here, the strong 0.7 preference appears in failure-only cases, suggesting the CPT may be too decisive and may underrepresent other explanations when physical anomaly evidence coexists with uncertainty elsewhere.

Column 0 corresponds to Network_Manipulation=Yes, Execution_Integrity=Compromised, Physical_Anomaly=Yes. Memory_Corruption is selected only weakly as argmax, but its failure-only activation suggests the class balance in this mixed-evidence setting may be off. Because this is the final decision CPT, even modest misallocation here can produce repeated wrong diagnoses.

cpt_danger_report.overall_summary: Execution_Integrity has the strongest independent evidence for refinement because repeated failures concentrate on its fusion logic, especially the all-clear Normal column and the partially supported Compromised column. Root_Causes is also a plausible refinement candidate because several final-class assignments are activated only in failures, indicating possible overconfident class mapping at the diagnosis layer. Upstream candidates such as Deviation_in_Response, Deviation_in_Dispatch, Program_Anomaly, and Network_Manipulation have weaker independent evidence because their suspicious activations are either semantically reasonable, substantially shared with successes, or better explained by downstream fusion/decision CPTs.

dangerous_cpts.main_problem: This CPT shows the strongest independent evidence of contributing to repeated failures. The activated parameter is used often in failures (7) and less often in successes (4), and it sits at a critical aggregation point between program/log deviations and the final diagnosis. The suspicious column corresponds to Program_Anomaly=Yes, Deviation_in_Response=No, Deviation_in_Dispatch=No, where the CPT gives only a tied 0.5 argmax for Compromised. In this domain, an inconsistent execution log alone is meaningful evidence of execution compromise or memory corruption, so such a weak/ambiguous assignment can plausibly suppress or destabilize downstream diagnosis across multiple failure cases. Its repeated appearance in common failure activation patterns with Root_Causes further supports that this CPT may independently distort the causal path rather than merely reflecting upstream evidence.

suspicious_parameters.justification: Column 3 is repeatedly activated in failures and represents the case where program anomaly is present without supporting response/dispatch deviations. Given the DER domain, application-log inconsistency can indicate software compromise even when physical or message-chain deviations are absent. Assigning only 0.5 to Compromised makes the node too indecisive at a key fusion point, which can propagate to incorrect root-cause selection.

cpt_danger_report.overall_summary: Execution_Integrity is the only CPT with sufficiently strong independent evidence for refinement. Network_Manipulation appears in some failures, but its failure/success contrast is weak and its high probability is domain-plausible for inconsistent network packets. Root_Causes is downstream and suspicious activations are better explained by ambiguity entering from Execution_Integrity; its statistics are not strong enough to show an independent modeling error.

dangerous_cpts.main_problem: The same Execution_Integrity parameter is repeatedly activated across four failure scenarios with very limited support from successful scenarios, and it sits on the key causal path from program/local deviations to the final diagnosis. Column 7 corresponds to Program_Anomaly=No, Deviation_in_Response=No, Deviation_in_Dispatch=No, yet the CPT strongly selects Normal (0.9). In this domain, repeated misclassification under an all-clear execution pattern is plausible if upstream evidence is incomplete or noisy; a very strong Normal assignment can then suppress Memory_Corruption or other execution-related diagnoses at the root node. This CPT therefore has independent leverage over final predictions and is not just a passive reflection of upstream evidence.

suspicious_parameters.justification: This parameter is the most recurrent failure-associated activation pattern and has a strong deterministic preference. Because Execution_Integrity is a direct parent of Root_Causes, an overly confident Normal assignment can independently bias the diagnosis away from execution-compromise explanations when evidence nodes fail to fire.

cpt_danger_report.overall_summary: Execution_Integrity is the only CPT with sufficiently strong independent evidence for refinement. Program_Anomaly shows some failure association, but its signal is weaker because the same parameter also appears in several successful scenarios and its behavior is largely upstream of the more influential Execution_Integrity node. Root_Causes parameters appear failure-associated, but their activations are plausibly downstream consequences of the Execution_Integrity pattern rather than independent evidence of flawed root-cause probabilities.
